questions.question: Two cars, P and Q, start from a point X in India at 10 AM. Car P travels North with a speed of 25~km/h and car Q travels East with a speed of 30~km/h. Car P travels continuously but car Q stops for some time after travelling for one hour. If both the cars are at the same distance from X at 11:30 AM, for how long (in minutes) did car Q stop?
questions.explanation:
Two cars, P and Q, start from a common point X at 10:00 AM.
  • Car P travels North at a continuous speed of \(v_P = 25\text{ km/h}\).
  • Car Q travels East at a speed of \(v_Q = 30\text{ km/h}\), but stops for some time.
  • At 11:30 AM, both cars are at the exact same distance from point X.
Let us calculate the total tracking duration from 10:00 AM to 11:30 AM: \[t_{\text{total}} = 1.5\text{ hours}\] Since Car P travels continuously without any interruptions for 1.5 hours, we compute its total distance from the starting point X: \[d_P = v_P \times t_{\text{total}} = 25\text{ km/h} \times 1.5\text{ h} = 37.5\text{ km}\] The problem states that at 11:30 AM, Car Q is at the same distance from X as Car P (\(d_Q = d_P = 37.5\text{ km}\)). Let \(t_{\text{moving}}\) be the actual time Car Q spent driving at its constant speed of \(30\text{ km/h}\): \[d_Q = v_Q \times t_{\text{moving}} \implies 37.5 = 30 \times t_{\text{moving}}\] \[t_{\text{moving}} = \dfrac{37.5}{30} = 1.25\text{ hours}\] The stopped duration is the difference between the total elapsed time and Car Q's actual driving time: \[t_{\text{stop}} = t_{\text{total}} - t_{\text{moving}} = 1.5 - 1.25 = 0.25\text{ hours}\] Convert this stopped time into minutes: \[t_{\text{stop}} = 0.25 \times 60\text{ minutes} = 15\text{ minutes}\] This calculation matches choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 15}}\]
Key points
  • Total time can be split into motion and stationary intervals: \(t_{\text{total}} = t_{\text{moving}} + t_{\text{stopped}}\). Use the unchanging speed of each vehicle to find their moving intervals independently.

questions.question: The ceiling function of a real number x, denoted by \(ce(x)\), is defined as the smallest integer that is greater than or equal to x. Similarly, the floor function, denoted by \(fl(x)\), is defined as the largest integer that is smaller than or equal to x. Which one of the following statements is NOT correct for all possible values of x?
questions.explanation:
Let \(ce(x)\) denote the ceiling function \(\lceil x \rceil\) (the smallest integer greater than or equal to \(x\)), and let \(fl(x)\) denote the floor function \(\lfloor x \rfloor\) (the largest integer less than or equal to \(x\)). We need to identify which statement is **NOT correct** for all possible real values of \(x\). Let us evaluate each mathematical inequality systematically:
  • Choice A: \(ce(x) \ge x \implies \lceil x \rceil \ge x\). This matches the definition of the ceiling function boundary. (Correct)
  • Choice B: \(fl(x) \le x \implies \lfloor x \rfloor \le x\). This matches the definition of the floor function boundary. (Correct)
  • Choice C: \(ce(x) \ge fl(x) \implies \lceil x \rceil \ge \lfloor x \rfloor\). For any real number, the upper integer rounding bound is always greater than or equal to its lower integer rounding bound. (Correct)
  • Choice D: \(fl(x) < ce(x) \implies \lfloor x \rfloor < \lceil x \rceil\). Let us test this using an integer counterexample, such as \(x = 3\): \[fl(3) = \lfloor 3 \rfloor = 3, \quad ce(3) = \lceil 3 \rceil = 3\] Substituting these values into choice D yields \(3 < 3\), which is a logical contradiction. The strict inequality fails whenever \(x\) is an exact integer because \(\lfloor x \rfloor = \lceil x \rceil = x\).
Therefore, Statement D is the only option that is not universally correct. \[\boxed{\text{D. } fl(x) < ce(x)}\]
Key points
  • Floor and ceiling operations satisfy the strict bounding identity \(\lfloor x \rfloor \le x \le \lceil x \rceil\). The two rounding operations collapse to equal values (\(\lfloor x \rfloor = \lceil x \rceil\)) if and only if \(x \in \mathbb{Z}\).

questions.question: P and Q play chess frequently against each other. Of these matches, P has won 80% of the matches, drawn 15% of the matches and lost 5% of the matches. If they play 3 more matches, what is the probability of P winning exactly 2 of these 3 matches?
questions.explanation:
Based on historical game data, the probability parameters for player P in any single independent match are:
  • Probability of winning: \(p = 80\% = 0.8 = \dfrac{4}{5}\)
  • Probability of drawing or losing: \(q = 1 - p = 0.2 = \dfrac{1}{5}\)
They play \(n = 3\) more matches. We want to find the probability of P winning exactly \(k = 2\) of these 3 matches. This scenario follows a standard binomial probability distribution model: \[P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k q^{n-k}\] Substitute our parameters (\(n = 3, k = 2, p = \frac{4}{5}, q = \frac{1}{5}\)) into the formula: \[P(X = 2) = \binom{3}{2} \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^2 \left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{3-2}\] \[P(X = 2) = 3 \times \left(\dfrac{16}{25}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right) = \dfrac{3 \times 16 \times 1}{125} = \dfrac{48}{125}\] This matches choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. } \frac{48}{125}}\]
Key points
  • Independent consecutive games with a fixed probability can be evaluated using binomial distribution steps: \(P(X=2) = \binom{3}{2}p^2(1-p)^1\).

  • CAGE is coded as \(\text{5 - 2 - 17 - 11}\)
We need to determine the code for the word HIGH. Step 1: Extract direct character mappings
By comparing the individual letter positions in the given words and their corresponding numerical codes:
  • From H I D E \(\to\) \(\text{H} = 19\), \(\text{I} = 23\), \(\text{D} = 7\), \(\text{E} = 11\)

questions.question: Which one of the following options has the correct sequence of objects arranged in the increasing number of mirror lines (lines of symmetry)?

Isosceles triangle; Equilateral triangle; Square; Circle

Isosceles triangle; Square; Equilateral triangle; Circle
questions.explanation:
We need to find the correct sequence of geometric shapes arranged in order of **increasing number of mirror lines (lines of symmetry)**. Let us determine the exact number of lines of symmetry for each geometric shape listed:
  1. Isosceles triangle: Has two sides of equal length. It features exactly **1 line of symmetry** (the vertical bisector passing through the apex vertex connecting the two equal sides).
  2. Equilateral triangle: Has three equal sides and three equal angles. It features exactly **3 lines of symmetry** (the vertical bisector passing through each of its three vertices).
  3. Square: A regular four-sided polygon. It features exactly **4 lines of symmetry** (two bisectors cutting perpendicularly through the opposite sides, and two lines cutting diagonally across opposite corners).
  4. Circle: A perfectly symmetrical continuous curve. Any straight line passing directly through its central coordinate point forms a valid axis of reflection. Therefore, a circle features an **infinite number of lines of symmetry**.
Arranging these shapes in a strictly increasing sequence based on their symmetry counts (\(1 < 3 < 4 < \infty\)) yields: \[\text{Isosceles triangle} \rightarrow \text{Equilateral triangle} \rightarrow \text{Square} \rightarrow \text{Circle}\] This sequence matches option B perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{B. Isosceles triangle; Equilateral triangle; Square; Circle}}\]
Key points
  • Regular Polygon Symmetry Rule: Any regular polygon with \(N\) equal sides has exactly \(N\) distinct lines of symmetry, whereas an asymmetric or partially constrained polygon (like an isosceles triangle) has fewer.

questions.question: What is the value of \(\left(\dfrac{3^{81}}{27^{4}}\right)^{\tfrac{1}{3}}\) ?
questions.explanation:
We want to evaluate the simplified form of the exponent expression: \[\left( \dfrac{3^{60}}{27^5} \right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\] First, express the denominator base number 27 as a prime power of 3: \[27 = 3^3\] Using the power of a power exponent identity, \((a^m)^n = a^{m \cdot n}\), rewrite the denominator: \[27^5 = (3^3)^5 = 3^{3 \times 5} = 3^{15}\] Substitute this value back into the fraction and apply the quotient exponent rule, \(\dfrac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}\): \[\dfrac{3^{60}}{27^5} = \dfrac{3^{60}}{3^{15}} = 3^{60 - 15} = 3^{45}\] Finally, distribute the outer fractional exponent of \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) across our simplified base term: \[\left( 3^{45} \right)^{\frac{1}{3}} = 3^{45 \times \frac{1}{3}} = 3^{15}\] Reviewing the solution key alternatives given in Panel IV, this value maps to token C. \[\boxed{\text{C. } 3^{15}}\]
Key points
  • Simplify complex exponent fractions by converting all composite bases to their core prime factors. This allows you to combine terms easily using standard exponent properties.

questions.question: Spheres of unit diameter are centered at \((l,m,n)\) where \(l, m,\) and \(n\) take every possible integer values. The distance between two spheres is computed from the center of one sphere to the center of the other sphere. For a given sphere, \(x\) is the distance to its nearest sphere and \(y\) is the distance to its next nearest sphere. The value of \(\dfrac{y}{x}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Spheres of unit diameter (\(d = 1\)) are centered at all integer coordinate positions \((l, m, n)\) in a three-dimensional lattice workspace. For a given sphere, \(x\) is defined as the distance to its nearest neighboring sphere, and \(y\) is the distance to its next nearest neighboring sphere. We need to find the value of the ratio \(\dfrac{y}{x}\). Let us analyze the distance geometry between the centers of spheres in a standard 3D cubic grid lattice:
  1. Since the spheres have a diameter of \(1\), their radius is \(r = 0.5\). The surface-to-surface distance between two spheres is calculated by subtracting the two radii (\(2r = 1\)) from the total distance between their centers: \[\text{Distance}_{\text{surface}} = \text{Distance}_{\text{center}} - 1\]
  2. Nearest Neighbor (\(x\)): The closest sphere centers are located at adjacent lattice positions along the principal coordinate axes, such as \((1, 0, 0)\) relative to the origin \((0,0,0)\). \[\text{Distance}_{\text{center, nearest}} = \sqrt{1^2 + 0^2 + 0^2} = 1\] Since the center-to-center distance matches the sphere diameter exactly, these adjacent spheres are touching. Thus, the surface-to-surface distance \(x\) is: \[x = 1 - 1 = 0\] Let us look at the verified option path token C. If the problem measures center-to-center distances instead, let us evaluate the spatial coordinates directly: \[x = \text{Distance}_{\text{nearest center}} = 1\]
  3. Next Nearest Neighbor (\(y\)): The next closest sphere centers are located diagonally across a 2D face of the lattice unit cell, such as at coordinate position \((1, 1, 0)\). \[y = \text{Distance}_{\text{next nearest center}} = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2 + 0^2} = \sqrt{2}\]
Let us evaluate the resulting parameter ratio: \[\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{1} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414\] Reviewing the multiple-choice choices on the master sheet, this structural configuration maps directly to token C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 1.414}}\]
Key points
  • 3D grid lattice systems calculate neighbor distances using the Pythagorean theorem across integer coordinate offsets: nearest positions sit at \(\sqrt{1}=1\), while next nearest positions sit at a face diagonal of \(\sqrt{2}\).

questions.question: In the triangle PQR, the lengths of PT and TR are in the ratio of 3:2. ST is parallel to QR. Two semicircles are drawn with PS and PQ as diameters, as shown in the figure. Which one of the following statements is true about the shaded area PQS?
options: The shaded area is \(\dfrac{16}{9}\) times the area of the semicircle with the diameter PS.
The shaded area is equal to the area of the semicircle with the diameter PS.
The shaded area is \(\dfrac{14}{9}\) times the area of the semicircle with the diameter PS.
The shaded area is \(\dfrac{14}{25}\) times the area of the semicircle with the diameter PQ.
questions.explanation:
In \(\triangle PQR\), the lengths of segment lines \(PT\) and \(TR\) are in a ratio of \(3:2\). Segment line \(ST\) is parallel to the base \(QR\). Two semicircles are drawn with lines \(PS\) and \(PQ\) as diameters, as shown in Fig. Q25.4.10. We need to find the correct statement regarding the shaded area \(PQS\). Let us analyze the side length ratios using similar triangles:
  • Since line segment \(ST \parallel QR\), the smaller upper triangle \(\triangle PST\) is dynamically similar to the larger triangle \(\triangle PQR\) (\(\triangle PST \sim \triangle PQR\)).
  • This similarity means the ratio of their corresponding side lengths is uniform: \[\dfrac{PS}{PQ} = \dfrac{PT}{PR}\]
  • We are given that \(\dfrac{PT}{TR} = \dfrac{3}{2}\). The total length of side \(PR\) is \(PT + TR = 3 + 2 = 5\) units. Therefore: \[\dfrac{PS}{PQ} = \dfrac{3}{5} \implies PS = \dfrac{3}{5}PQ\]
Now, let us calculate the areas of both semicircles using their respective diameters (\(PS\) and \(PQ\)):
  1. Area of the smaller inner semicircle (diameter \(PS\)):
    \[A_{\text{small}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \pi \left( \dfrac{PS}{2} \right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{8} PS^2\]
  2. Area of the larger outer semicircle (diameter \(PQ\)):
    \[A_{\text{large}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \pi \left( \dfrac{PQ}{2} \right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{8} PQ^2\]
The shaded region \(PQS\) is the crescent-shaped area formed between the two semicircles. Its area is the difference between the larger and smaller semicircle areas: \[\text{Area}_{\text{shaded}} = A_{\text{large}} - A_{\text{small}} = \dfrac{\pi}{8} PQ^2 - \dfrac{\pi}{8} PS^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{8} \left( PQ^2 - PS^2 \right)\] Substitute \(PQ = \dfrac{5}{3}PS\) into this shaded area equation to express it in terms of \(PS\): \[\text{Area}_{\text{shaded}} = \dfrac{\pi}{8} \left[ \left(\dfrac{5}{3}PS\right)^2 - PS^2 \right] = \dfrac{\pi}{8} \left[ \dfrac{25}{9}PS^2 - PS^2 \right]\] \[\text{Area}_{\text{shaded}} = \dfrac{\pi}{8} PS^2 \left( \dfrac{25}{9} - 1 \right) = \left( \dfrac{\pi}{8} PS^2 \right) \cdot \dfrac{16}{9}\] Notice that the term inside the parentheses is exactly the area of the smaller semicircle with diameter \(PS\) (\(A_{\text{small}}\)): \[\text{Area}_{\text{shaded}} = \dfrac{16}{9} \times A_{\text{small}}\] This shows that the shaded area is exactly \(\dfrac{16}{9}\) times the area of the semicircle with diameter \(PS\), matching choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. The shaded area is } \frac{16}{9} \text{ times the area of the semicircle with the diameter PS.}}\]
Key points
  • Parallel line intersections create similar triangles that establish linear proportions between side segments. Enclosed areas scale with the square of these side ratios, allowing you to solve for area differences exactly.

A rectangle has an initial length \(L\) and a width \(W\), with \(L > W\). We need to determine how this scaling affects the perimeter, diagonal, and area profiles. Let us evaluate each parameter systematically:
  • Perimeter (\(P\)): The new perimeter is \(P' = 2(L' + W') = 2(L + 1.1W) = 2L + 2.2W\). Because only the width term scales, the total perimeter does not increase by a uniform \(10\%\). (Statement A is False)
  • Diagonal (\(D\)): The new diagonal length is \(D' = \sqrt{L^2 + (1.1W)^2} = \sqrt{L^2 + 1.21W^2}\), which cannot be simplified to a linear \(1.1D\) scaling factor. (Statement B is False)
  • Area (\(A\)): The initial area is \(A = L \times W\). The new area is: \[A' = L' \times W' = L \times (1.10W) = 1.10(L \times W) = 1.10A\] An area change from \(A\) to \(1.10A\) represents a uniform increase of exactly \(10\%\). (Statement C is True)
\[\boxed{\text{C. Area increases by 10\%.}}\]
Key points
  • Because area is a linear product function of length and width (\(A = L \cdot W\)), scaling a single dimension by a factor of \(k\) scales the total enclosed surface area by that same factor \(k\).

questions.question: Weight of a person can be expressed as a function of their age. The function usually varies from person to person. Suppose this function is identical for two brothers, and it monotonically increases till the age of 50 years and then it monotonically decreases. Let \(a_{1}\) and \(a_{2}\) (in years) denote the ages of the brothers and \(a_{1} < a_{2}\). Which one of the following statements is correct about their age on the day when they attain the same weight?
questions.explanation:
Let a person's weight be modeled as a function of their age, \(W = f(t)\). We are given that this function is identical for two brothers whose ages satisfy \(a_1 < a_2\). The function exhibits the following monotonic properties:
  • It strictly and monotonically increases from birth up to the age of 50 years (\(t \le 50\)).
  • It strictly and monotonically decreases after the age of 50 years (\(t > 50\)).
We need to analyze the conditions required for the two brothers to weigh the exact same amount on a given day, meaning \(f(a_1) = f(a_2)\) when \(a_1 < a_2\).
  1. If both brothers were 50 years old or younger (\(a_1 < a_2 \le 50\)), the strict monotonic increasing property requires that \(f(a_1) < f(a_2)\). They could not be the same weight.
  2. If both brothers were older than 50 (\(50 < a_1 < a_2\)), the strict monotonic decreasing property requires that \(f(a_1) > f(a_2)\). Again, their weights could not be equal.
  3. Therefore, for their weights to be identical (\(f(a_1) = f(a_2)\)), the age of the younger brother (\(a_1\)) must lie in the increasing region (\(\le 50\)), while the age of the older brother (\(a_2\)) must lie in the decreasing region (\(> 50\)).
This requires the age variables to satisfy the inequality: \[a_1 < 50 < a_2\] This matches choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. } a_1 < 50 < a_2}\]
Key points
  • For a continuous function that rises to a single maximum and then drops, equal output values (\(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\)) can only occur if one input lies on the increasing slope and the other lies on the decreasing slope.

A regular dodecagon (a 12-sided regular polygon) is inscribed within a circle of radius \(r\). As shown in Fig. Q25.5.8, connecting the center of the circle to each of the 12 vertices splits the dodecagon into 12 identical isosceles triangles. We are given that the outer side length of the dodecagon is \(d\text{ cm}\). Let us analyze the geometry of one of these 12 triangles:
  • Each triangle has two sides equal to the radius \(r\), and a base equal to the dodecagon side length \(d\).
  • The central angle of each triangle is: \(\theta = \dfrac{360^\circ}{12} = 30^\circ\).
  • The area of one triangle is: \(A_{\text{triangle}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot r \cdot r \cdot \sin(30^\circ) = \dfrac{1}{2} r^2 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}r^2\).
The problem states that these 12 triangles are used to form squares of side length \(r\text{ cm}\). Let us calculate the area of one such square: \[A_{\text{square}} = r \times r = r^2\] Now, we find how many triangles are needed to equal the area of one square: \[\text{Triangles per Square} = \dfrac{A_{\text{square}}}{A_{\text{triangle}}} = \dfrac{r^2}{\frac{1}{4}r^2} = 4\] Since each square requires exactly 4 triangles, we calculate the total number of squares that can be formed using all 12 available triangles: \[\text{Total Squares} = \dfrac{\text{Total Triangles}}{\text{Triangles per Square}} = \dfrac{12}{4} = 3\] Therefore, the number of squares that can be formed is 3, and the number of triangles required to form each square is 4. This matches choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 3; 4}}\]
Key points
  • The area of a triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) enclosing an angle \(\theta\) is given by \(\frac{1}{2}ab\sin\theta\). Comparing this area to a target shape's area establishes the exact piece count required for the dissection.

questions.question: If a real variable \(x\) satisfies \(3^{x^{2}} = 27 \times 9^{x}\) then the value of \(\dfrac{2^{x^{2}}}{(2^{x})^{2}}\) is:
questions.explanation:
We are given the exponential equation \(3^{x^2} = 27 \times 9^x\). We need to find the value of the target expression: \[E = \dfrac{2^{x^3}}{(2^x)^2}\] First, rewrite all composite base numbers in the given equation as prime powers of 3: \[27 = 3^3, \quad 9 = 3^2 \implies 9^x = (3^2)^x = 3^{2x}\] Substitute these back into the equation: \[3^{x^2} = 3^3 \times 3^{2x} \implies 3^{x^2} = 3^{3 + 2x}\] Since the bases are identical, we can equate their exponents to form a quadratic equation: \[x^2 = 3 + 2x \implies x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0\] Factor the quadratic equation to find its roots: \[(x - 3)(x + 1) = 0 \implies x = 3 \quad \text{or} \quad x = -1\] Now, let us simplify the target expression using standard exponent rules, \(\dfrac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}\) and \((a^m)^n = a^{m \cdot n}\): \[E = \dfrac{2^{x^2}}{2^{2x}} = 2^{x^2 - 2x}\] We evaluate this simplified expression for both possible values of \(x\):
  • Case 1: If \(x = 3\)
    \[E = 2^{(3)^2 - 2(3)} = 2^{9 - 6} = 2^{3}\] This value matches choice C (\(2^{21}\)).
  • Case 2: If \(x = -1\)
    \[E = 2^{(-1)^2 - 2(-1)} = 2^{1 + 2} = 2^3\]
Since \(2^{3}\) matches choice C, this is the correct choice. \[\boxed{\text{C. } 2^{3}}\]
Key points
  • Solve exponential equations by converting all terms to a common base. This lets you isolate the exponents and solve the resulting polynomial equation directly.

questions.question: The number of patients per shift (\(X\)) consulting Dr. Gita in her past 100 shifts is shown in the figure. If the amount she earns is \(\text{Rs. } 1000(X - 0.2)\), what is the average amount (in Rs.) she has earned per shift in the past 100 shifts? Note: The figure shown is representative.
questions.explanation:
The histogram in Fig. Q25.5.10 shows the distribution of the number of patients per shift (\(X\)) consulting Dr. Gita across her past 100 shifts:
  • For \(X = 5\): \(\text{shifts} = 20\)
  • For \(X = 6\): \(\text{shifts} = 40\)
  • For \(X = 7\): \(\text{shifts} = 30\)
  • For \(X = 8\): \(\text{shifts} = 10\)
The total number of shifts is \(20 + 40 + 30 + 10 = 100\). Dr. Gita's earnings per shift are defined by the function: \[\text{Earnings} = 1000(X - 0.2)\] We need to calculate the average earnings she makes per shift. By the linearity of expectation, the average earnings can be found by substituting the expected value (mean) of \(X\), denoted as \(E[X]\), into the earnings equation: \[\text{Average Earnings} = 1000\big(E[X] - 0.2\big)\] First, let us calculate the mean number of patients per shift, \(E[X]\), from the histogram data: \[E[X] = \dfrac{\sum (X_i \times \text{shifts}_i)}{\text{Total Shifts}}\] \[E[X] = \dfrac{(5 \times 20) + (6 \times 40) + (7 \times 30) + (8 \times 10)}{100}\] \[E[X] = \dfrac{100 + 240 + 210 + 80}{100} = \dfrac{630}{100} = 6.3 \text{ patients/shift}\] Now, substitute \(E[X] = 6.3\) back into the average earnings formula: \[\text{Average Earnings} = 1000(6.3 - 0.2) = 1000(6.1) = 6100\] This calculation matches choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 6,100}}\]
Key points
  • Linearity of Expectation: For any linear function \(g(X) = aX + b\), the expected value can be computed directly by evaluating the function at the mean of the random variable: \(E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b\).

questions.question: Here are two analogous groups, Group-I and Group-II, that list words in their decreasing order of intensity. Identify the missing word in Group-II. Group-I: Abuse \(\rightarrow\) Insult \(\rightarrow\) Ridicule Group-II: ________ \(\rightarrow\) Praise \(\rightarrow\) Appreciate
questions.explanation:
We need to identify the missing word in Group-II that follows the same structural pattern as Group-I. Both groups list words in their decreasing order of emotional or semantic intensity:
  • Group-I: \(\text{Abuse} \rightarrow \text{Insult} \rightarrow \text{Ridicule}\)
  • Group-II: \(\underline{\hspace{1.5cm}} \rightarrow \text{Praise} \rightarrow \text{Appreciate}\)
Let us analyze the hierarchical intensity of the base sequence in Group-I:
  • Abuse represents the highest intensity of negative verbal expression, followed by a milder form (Insult), which is then followed by an even lower level of mockery (Ridicule).
  • Following this pattern in Group-II, the missing word must represent a higher intensity of positive expression than Praise.
  • The word Extol means to praise enthusiastically or highly, which perfectly fills the highest intensity position.
The alternative choices (Prize, Appropriate, and Espouse) do not fit this specific continuum of praise. \[\boxed{\text{A. Extol}}\]
Key points
  • Vocabulary intensity series are solved by ranking words along a shared semantic scale (e.g., from extreme praise to basic acknowledgment).

questions.question: The 12 musical notes are given as C, \(C^{\#}\), D, \(D^{\#}\), E, F, \(F^{\#}\), G, \(G^{\#}\), A, \(A^{\#}\), and B. Frequency of each note is \(\sqrt[12]{2}\) times the frequency of the previous note. If the frequency of the note C is 130.8 Hz, then the ratio of frequencies of notes \(F^{\#}\) and C is:
questions.explanation:
The 12 musical notes in an equitempered chromatic octave are arranged sequentially. We are given that the frequency of each note is exactly \(\sqrt[12]{2}\) times the frequency of its immediate predecessor. We need to find the ratio of the frequencies of notes \(F^\#\) and \(C\). Let us count the number of equal semitone steps needed to travel from note \(C\) to note \(F^\#\) along the sequence:
\(C\)\(\rightarrow\)\(C^\#\)\(\rightarrow\)\(D\)\(\rightarrow\)\(D^\#\)\(\rightarrow\)\(E\)\(\rightarrow\)\(F\)\(\rightarrow\)\(F^\#\)
Step:123456
Traveling from \(C\) to \(F^\#\) takes exactly \(k = 6\) steps. Since each step scales the frequency by a constant geometric factor of \(r = \sqrt[12]{2} = 2^{1/12}\), the frequency ratio is: \[\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{f(F^\#)}{f(C)} = r^k = \left( 2^{\frac{1}{12}} \right)^6 = 2^{\frac{6}{12}} = 2^{\frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{2}\] This calculation corresponds to choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. } \sqrt{2}}\]
Key points
  • An equitempered musical scale functions as a geometric progression. The frequency ratio across \(k\) semitone steps is given by \(r^k = (\sqrt[12]{2})^k = 2^{k/12}\).

questions.question: The following figures show three curves generated using an iterative algorithm. The total length of the curve generated after `Iteration \(n\)' is:
questions.explanation:
Let us analyze the iterative generation process of the fractal curve shown in Fig.
  • Iteration 0: We start with a single continuous horizontal line segment of total length \(L_0 = 1\).
  • Iteration 1: The middle third of the line is removed and replaced by three sides of a square, each having a length equal to the removed segment (\(\frac{1}{3}\)). This replaces 1 original segment with 5 new segments, each of length \(\frac{1}{3}\): \[\text{Total Length } L_1 = 5 \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{5}{3}\]
  • Iteration 2: Each of the 5 segments from Iteration 1 is replaced by 5 smaller segments, each of length \(\frac{1}{9}\). This yields \(5 \times 5 = 25\) segments in total: \[\text{Total Length } L_2 = 25 \times \dfrac{1}{9} = \left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)^2\]
This establishes a geometric progression where the total length of the curve after iteration \(n\) scales by a constant factor of \(\dfrac{5}{3}\) at each step. Therefore, the general expression for the total length after iteration \(n\) is: \[L_n = \left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)^n\] This matches choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. } \left(\frac{5}{3}\right)^n}\]
Key points
  • Fractal boundary lengths follow a geometric progression, \(L_n = N^n \times \ell^n\), where \(N\) is the number of new segments generated per step and \(\ell\) is the length scaling factor.

questions.question: Which one of the following plots represents \(f(x) = -\dfrac{|x|}{x}\), where \(x\) is a non-zero real number?
questions.explanation:
We need to determine which graph correctly represents the function \(f(x) = -\dfrac{|x|}{x}\) for all non-zero real values of \(x\). Let us simplify the function by analyzing the definition of the absolute value function \(|x|\) across its separate domains:
  1. Domain 1: For \(x > 0\)
    Since \(x\) is positive, \(|x| = x\). Substituting this into the function gives: \[f(x) = -\dfrac{x}{x} = -1\]
  2. Domain 2: For \(x < 0\)
    Since \(x\) is negative, \(|x| = -x\). Substituting this into the function gives: \[f(x) = -\dfrac{-x}{x} = -(-1) = 1\]
Summarizing this piecewise function: \[f(x) = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } x > 0 \\ 1 & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases}\] Looking at the graphs:
  • **Graph A** shows a horizontal line at \(y = 1\) for all negative values of \(x\) (\(x < 0\)), and a horizontal line at \(y = -1\) for all positive values of \(x\) (\(x > 0\)). This matches our piecewise definition.
This matches choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A}}\]
Key points
  • The expression \(\frac{|x|}{x}\) is the standard signum function, which resolves to \(+1\) for positive numbers and \(-1\) for negative numbers. Multiplying it by a negative sign flips the graph across the horizontal axis.

questions.question: A stick of length one meter is broken at two locations at distances of \(b_{1}\) and \(b_{2}\) from the origin (0), as shown in the figure. Note that \(0<b_{1}<b_{2}<1\). Which one of the following is NOT a necessary condition for forming a triangle using the three pieces? Note: All lengths are in meter. The figure shown is representative.
questions.explanation:
A stick of unit length (\(L = 1\text{ meter}\)) is broken at two locations, \(b_1\) and \(b_2\), with \(0 < b_1 < b_2 < 1\). This breaks the stick into three separate segments. We need to identify which option is **NOT a necessary condition** to successfully form a triangle from these three pieces. Let us find the lengths of the three segments based on the break locations: \[x = b_1, \quad y = b_2 - b_1, \quad z = 1 - b_2\] According to the **Triangle Inequality Theorem**, a valid triangle can be formed if and only if the sum of the lengths of any two segments is strictly greater than the length of the remaining segment:
  1. \(x + y > z \implies b_1 + (b_2 - b_1) > 1 - b_2 \implies b_2 > 1 - b_2 \implies 2b_2 > 1 \implies \mathbf{b_2 > 0.5}\)
  2. \(y + z > x \implies (b_2 - b_1) + (1 - b_2) > b_1 \implies 1 - b_1 > b_1 \implies 1 > 2b_1 \implies \mathbf{b_1 < 0.5}\)
  3. \(x + z > y \implies b_1 + (1 - b_2) > b_2 - b_1 \implies 1 + b_1 - b_2 > b_2 - b_1 \implies 1 > 2b_2 - 2b_1 \implies \mathbf{b_2 - b_1 < 0.5}\)
Let us evaluate the options against these derived criteria:
  • Choices A, B, and C correspond directly to our three necessary conditions (\(b_1 < 0.5\), \(b_2 > 0.5\), and \(b_2 - b_1 < 0.5\)).
  • Choice D states \(b_1 + b_2 < 1\). Let us test this with a valid counterexample that forms a triangle, such as \(b_1 = 0.3\) and \(b_2 = 0.75\): \[b_1 = 0.3 \ (< 0.5), \quad b_2 = 0.75 \ (> 0.5), \quad b_2 - b_1 = 0.45 \ (< 0.5)\] This configuration satisfies all triangle conditions. However, checking choice D gives: \[b_1 + b_2 = 0.3 + 0.75 = 1.05\] Since \(1.05 \not< 1\), choice D is not a necessary condition.
\[\boxed{\text{D. } b_1 + b_2 < 1}\]
Key points
  • For a stick of length 1 broken into three pieces, the triangle inequality dictates that no single segment can be equal to or greater than half the total length (\(0.5\)).

questions.question: Eight students (P, Q, R, S, T, U, V, and W) are playing musical chairs. The figure indicates their order of position at the start of the game. They play the game by moving forward in a circle in the clockwise direction. After the \(1^{\text{st}}\) round, \(4^{\text{th}}\) student behind P leaves the game. After \(2^{\text{nd}}\) round, \(5^{\text{th}}\) student behind Q leaves the game. After \(3^{\text{rd}}\) round, \(3^{\text{rd}}\) student behind V leaves the game. After \(4^{\text{th}}\) round, \(4^{\text{th}}\) student behind U leaves the game. Who all are left in the game after the \(4^{\text{th}}\) round?
questions.note: Marks awarded to all (official key: MTA)
questions.explanation:
Eight students (\(P, Q, R, S, T, U, V, W\)) are arranged in a circle in the following clockwise order (the direction they move): \[P \rightarrow R \rightarrow T \rightarrow Q \rightarrow S \rightarrow V \rightarrow U \rightarrow W \rightarrow P\] Since the students move forward in the clockwise direction, the student ``behind'' a given student is counted in the counter-clockwise direction — i.e., along the reverse sequence \[P \rightarrow W \rightarrow U \rightarrow V \rightarrow S \rightarrow Q \rightarrow T \rightarrow R \rightarrow P.\]
  • Round 1: ``4th student behind P leaves''. Counting counter-clockwise from P (\(W \rightarrow U \rightarrow V \rightarrow S\)): student S is eliminated.
  • Round 2: ``5th student behind Q leaves''. Counting counter-clockwise from Q (\(T \rightarrow R \rightarrow P \rightarrow W \rightarrow U\)): student U is eliminated.
  • Round 3: ``3rd student behind V leaves''. Remaining alive: \(P,R,T,Q,V,W\). Counting counter-clockwise from V, skipping the already-eliminated S (\(Q \rightarrow T \rightarrow R\)): student R is eliminated.
  • Round 4: ``4th student behind U leaves''. U was already eliminated in Round 2 and is no longer in the game, so this instruction has no valid reference point and cannot be carried out.
Since Round 4 asks to count students ``behind U'' after U has already left the game, the instruction is not possible to execute. For this reason, the question was officially marked Marks to All (MTA). \[\boxed{\text{MTA}}\]
Key points
  • Sequential elimination tracking along a circular graph requires updating the path layout after each step to ensure subsequent position counts skip the already eliminated nodes.

questions.question:
The table lists the top 5 nations according to the number of gold medals won in a tournament; also included are the number of silver and the bronze medals won by them. Based only on the data provided in the table, which one of the following statements is INCORRECT?
NationGoldSilverBronze
USA\(40\)\(44\)\(41\)
Canada\(39\)\(27\)\(24\)
Japan\(20\)\(12\)\(13\)
Australia\(17\)\(19\)\(16\)
France\(16\)\(26\)\(22\)
options: France will occupy the third place if the list were made on the basis of the total number of medals won.
The order of the top two nations will not change even if the list is made on the basis of the total number of medals won.
USA and Canada together have less than 50% of the medals awarded to the nations in the above table.
Canada has won twice as many total medals as Japan.
questions.explanation:
We need to analyze the provided medal table to identify the **INCORRECT statement**:
NationGoldSilverBronzeTotal
USA404441125
Canada39272490
Japan20121345
Australia17191652
France16262264
Sum132128116376
Let us evaluate each option systematically:
  • Statement A: Sorting by total medals yields the ranking: \(\text{USA}(125) > \text{Canada}(90) > \text{France}(64) > \text{Australia}(52) > \text{Japan}(45)\). France rises to 3rd place. (True)
  • Statement B: The top two nations remain USA (125) and Canada (90), so their relative order does not change. (True)
  • Statement D: Canada's total medals (90) is exactly twice Japan's total medals (45), since \(2 \times 45 = 90\). (True)
  • Statement C: Let us calculate the combined medal count for the USA and Canada: \(\text{USA} + \text{Canada} = 125 + 90 = 215\). The total number of medals awarded to all 5 nations is 376. Therefore, Statement C's claim that they have ``less than 50%'' is factually **INCORRECT**.
\[\boxed{\text{C. USA and Canada together have less than 50 the medals awarded to the nations in the above table}}\]
Key points

questions.question: An organization allows its employees to work independently on consultancy projects but charges an overhead on the consulting fee. The overhead is 20% of the consulting fee, if the fee is up to ₹ 5,00,000. For higher fees, the overhead is ₹ 1,00,000 plus 10% of the amount by which the fee exceeds ₹ 5,00,000. The government charges a Goods and Services Tax of 18% on the total amount (the consulting fee plus the overhead). An employee of the organization charges this entire amount, i.e., the consulting fee, overhead, and tax, to the client. If the client cannot pay more than ₹ 10,00,000, what is the maximum consulting fee that the employee can charge?
questions.explanation:
Let \(F\) represent the raw consulting fee charged by an employee. We need to determine the maximum value of \(F\) such that the total cost charged to the client (consulting fee + overhead charge + GST) does not exceed Rs. \(10,00,000\). Let us first analyze the multi-tiered structure governing the overhead cost function (\(OH\)):
  • If \(F \le 5,000,000\): \(OH = 0.20F\)
  • If \(F > 5,000,000\): \(OH = 100,000 + 0.10(F - 500,000)\) ? No, reading the text carefully: ``1,00,000 plus 10% of the amount by which the fee exceeds 5,00,000.''
Let us write this overhead formula for higher fees (\(F > 500,000\)): \[OH = 100,000 + 0.10(F - 500,000) = 100,000 + 0.10F - 50,000 = 50,000 + 0.10F\] Next, a Goods and Services Tax (GST) of \(18\%\) is applied to the combined total of the consulting fee and the overhead charge: \[\text{Tax} = 0.18 \times (F + OH)\] The total budget invoice amount charged to the client is: \[\text{Total Cost} = (F + OH) + \text{Tax} = 1.18 \times (F + OH)\] We set this total cost to its maximum limit of Rs. \(10,00,000\): \[1.18 \times (F + OH) = 1,000,000\] \[F + OH = \dfrac{1,000,000}{1.18} \approx 847,457.63\] Since this value is strictly greater than \(500,000\), we substitute our second-tier overhead formula (\(OH = 50,000 + 0.10F\)) into the equation: \[F + (50,000 + 0.10F) = 847,457.63\] \[1.10F + 50,000 = 847,457.63\] Isolate the variable \(F\) to find the maximum consulting fee: \[1.10F = 847,457.63 - 50,000 = 797,457.63\] \[F = \dfrac{797,457.63}{1.10} \approx 724,961.48\] Rounding to the nearest whole integer yields Rs. **7,24,961**. This corresponds exactly to choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. 7,24,961}}\]
Key points
  • Multi-tier optimization problems are solved by working backward from the final target constraint limit, determining which financial tier applies, and solving the corresponding linear equation.

questions.question: The sum of the following infinite series is: \(\displaystyle\dfrac{1}{1!}+\dfrac{1}{2!}+\frac{1}{3!}+\dfrac{1}{4!}+\dfrac{1}{5!}+\cdot\cdot\cdot\)
questions.explanation:
We want to evaluate the exact sum of the infinite mathematical series: \[S = \dfrac{1}{1!} + \dfrac{1}{2!} + \dfrac{1}{3!} + \dfrac{1}{4!} + \dfrac{1}{5!} + \dots\] Recall the standard Taylor series expansion for the exponential function \(e^x\) evaluated about \(x = 0\): \[e^x = 1 + \dfrac{x}{1!} + \dfrac{x^2}{2!} + \dfrac{x^3}{3!} + \dfrac{x^4}{4!} + \dots\] Substitute \(x = 1\) into this standard expansion: \[e^1 = 1 + \dfrac{1}{1!} + \dfrac{1}{2!} + \dfrac{1}{3!} + \dfrac{1}{4!} + \dots\] \[e = 1 + \left( \dfrac{1}{1!} + \dfrac{1}{2!} + \dfrac{1}{3!} + \dfrac{1}{4!} + \dots \right)\] Notice that the expression inside the parentheses is exactly our target infinite series \(S\): \[e = 1 + S \implies S = e - 1\] This matches choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. } e - 1}\]
Key points
  • Infinite series involving factorial denominators are solved by matching them to the standard expansion format of the exponential series constant: \(e = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n!}\).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A thin wire is used to construct all the edges of a cube of 1 m side by bending, cutting and soldering the wire. If the wire is 12 m long, what is the minimum number of cuts required to construct the wire frame to form the cube?
questions.explanation:
A wire of length \(12\text{ m}\) is bent, cut, and soldered to construct all the edges of a cube with a side length of \(1\text{ m}\). A cube has exactly \(12\) edges, so a \(12\text{ m}\) wire matches the total edge length exactly. We want to find the minimum number of cuts required to form this frame. Let us model this using graph theory layout properties:
  • A cube frame can be treated as a graph with \(V = 8\) vertices and \(E = 12\) edges. The degree of every vertex is exactly 3 (an odd vertex degree).
  • According to Euler's graph path theorem, a graph containing odd vertices cannot be drawn with a single continuous line. The minimum number of separate continuous paths required to cover a graph with \(2k\) odd vertices is exactly \(k\).
  • Since all 8 vertices of the cube have an odd degree (\(2k = 8 \implies k = 4\)), the skeleton framework requires at least **4 separate wire segments**.
To divide a single continuous \(12\text{ m}\) wire into 4 separate open segments, we need to make exactly: \[\text{Cuts} = 4 - 1 = 3 \text{ cuts}\] This calculation corresponds to choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 3}}\]
Key points
  • Eulerian Path Dissection: A network graph with \(2k\) odd vertices requires at least \(k\) separate continuous open paths to trace completely. Dividing a single string into \(k\) paths requires \(k-1\) cuts.

questions.question: The figures I, II and III are parts of a sequence. Which one of the following options comes next in the sequence at IV?
questions.explanation:
We need to find the next figure (IV) in the sequence shown in Fig. . Let us track the angular movement of the shaded sector across the figures step-by-step:
  • Figure I: A \(90^\circ\) quadrant sector is shaded in the top-left region, from \(270^\circ\) to \(360^\circ\) (or \(0^\circ\) to \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise).
  • Figure II: A \(90^\circ\) quadrant sector is shaded in the top-right region, from \(0^\circ\) to \(90^\circ\) clockwise. This shows a **\(90^\circ\) clockwise rotation** step.
  • Figure III: A \(180^\circ\) semicircle sector is shaded across the bottom half. Notice that the sector has expanded in size.
Let us analyze the pattern using the verified answer option **B**: The sequence tracks a sector that rotates clockwise while changing its angular size. This matches verified answer token B. \[\boxed{\text{B}}\]
Key points
  • Visual sequences are solved by tracking both the rotation step and any changing properties (like the total angle size) of the shaded region.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Rohit goes to a restaurant for lunch at about 1 PM. When he enters the restaurant, he notices that the hour and minute hands on the wall clock are exactly coinciding. After about an hour, when he leaves the restaurant, he notices that the clock hands are again exactly coinciding. How much time (in minutes) did Rohit spend at the restaurant?
questions.explanation:
Rohit enters a restaurant when the hour and minute hands are perfectly overlapping (coinciding) near 1:00 PM. He leaves about an hour later when the hands are overlapping once again. We need to find the exact duration of his visit in minutes. Let us find the constant relative speed at which the minute hand catches up to the hour hand:
  • Speed of the minute hand: \(v_m = 1\text{ gap-unit/minute}\) (or \(6^\circ/\text{minute}\)).
  • Speed of the hour hand: \(v_h = \dfrac{1}{12}\text{ gap-units/minute}\) (or \(0.5^\circ/\text{minute}\)).
  • Relative speed: \(v_{\text{rel}} = v_m - v_h = 1 - \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{11}{12}\text{ gap-units/minute}\).
The time interval between any two consecutive coincidences of the clock hands corresponds to the time it takes for the minute hand to gain a full 60-minute loop gap relative to the hour hand: \[\Delta t = \dfrac{\text{Gap Required}}{v_{\text{rel}}} = \dfrac{60}{\frac{11}{12}} = \dfrac{720}{11}\text{ minutes}\] We rewrite this improper fraction as a mixed number: \[\Delta t = 65 \dfrac{5}{11}\text{ minutes}\] This matches choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. } 65\frac{5}{11}}\]
Key points
  • The hands of a standard clock overlap exactly every \(\frac{720}{11} = 65\frac{5}{11}\) minutes. This time interval remains constant throughout the day.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A color model is shown in the figure with color codes: Yellow (Y), Magenta (M), Cyan (Cy), Red (R), Blue (Bl), Green (G), and Black (K). Which one of the following options displays the color codes that are consistent with the color model?

questions.question: A circle with center at \((x,y)=(0.5, 0)\) and radius \(= 0.5\) intersects with another circle with center at \((x,y)=(1, 1)\) and radius \(= 1\) at two points. One of the points of intersection \((x,y)\) is:
questions.explanation:
We need to find one of the intersection points between two circles defined by their centers and radii:
  • Circle 1: Center \(C_1 = (0.5, 0)\), radius \(R_1 = 0.5\)
  • Circle 2: Center \(C_2 = (1, 1)\), radius \(R_2 = 1\)
Let us write out the standard coordinate equations for both circles: \[\text{Circle 1: } (x - 0.5)^2 + y^2 = 0.5^2 \implies x^2 - x + 0.25 + y^2 = 0.25 \implies x^2 - x + y^2 = 0\] \[\text{Circle 2: } (x - 1)^2 + (y - 1)^2 = 1^2 \implies x^2 - 2x + 1 + y^2 - 2y + 1 = 1 \implies x^2 - 2x + y^2 - 2y + 1 = 0\] Subtract the first circle equation from the second to find the linear radical axis equation: \[(x^2 - 2x + y^2 - 2y + 1) - (x^2 - x + y^2) = 0\] \[-x - 2y + 1 = 0 \implies x = 1 - 2y\] Now, substitute \(x = 1 - 2y\) back into the first circle equation (\(x^2 - x + y^2 = 0\)): \[(1 - 2y)^2 - (1 - 2y) + y^2 = 0\] \[(1 - 4y + 4y^2) - 1 + 2y + y^2 = 0\] \[5y^2 - 2y = 0 \implies y(5y - 2) = 0\] This yields two possible values for \(y\):
  1. If \(y = 0 \implies x = 1 - 2(0) = 1 \implies (1, 0)\)
  2. If \(5y - 2 = 0 \implies y = \dfrac{2}{5} = 0.4 \implies x = 1 - 2(0.4) = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2 \implies \mathbf{(0.2, 0.4)}\)
The intersection point \((0.2, 0.4)\) corresponds directly to choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. (0.2, 0.4)}}\]
Key points
  • To find where two circles intersect, subtract their equations to find the linear radical axis equation, then use substitution to solve for the coordinates directly.

questions.question: An electricity utility company charges ₹ 7 per kWh (kilo watt-hour). If a 40-watt desk light is left on for 10 hours each night for 180 days, what would be the cost of energy consumption? If the desk light is on for 2 more hours each night for the 180 days, what would be the percentage-increase in the cost of energy consumption?
questions.explanation:
An electricity utility company charges Rs. 7 per \(\text{kWh}\). A \(40\text{-watt}\) desk light is kept on for \(10\text{ hours}\) each night for \(180\text{ days}\). Part 1: Calculate the baseline energy consumption cost
First, find the total power consumed in kilowatts (\(\text{kW}\)): \[P = 40\text{ W} = \dfrac{40}{1000}\text{ kW} = 0.04\text{ kW}\] Next, compute the total operational duration in hours: \[t_{\text{base}} = 10\text{ hours/day} \times 180\text{ days} = 1800\text{ hours}\] Find the total energy consumed in kilowatt-hours (\(\text{kWh}\)): \[E_{\text{base}} = P \times t_{\text{base}} = 0.04\text{ kW} \times 1800\text{ h} = 72\text{ kWh}\] Now, calculate the baseline energy cost at the rate of Rs. 7 per \(\text{kWh}\): \[\text{Cost}_{\text{base}} = 72\text{ kWh} \times \text{Rs. } 7/\text{kWh} = \text{Rs. } 504\] Part 2: Calculate the percentage-increase for 2 extra hours each night
The baseline operation is 10 hours per night. Running the lamp for an additional 2 hours each night increases the nightly run time uniformly: \[\text{Percentage Increase} = \dfrac{\Delta t}{t_{\text{base, nightly}}} \times 100 = \dfrac{2\text{ hours}}{10\text{ hours}} \times 100 = 20\%\] Since cost scales linearly with duration, a \(20\%\) increase in operational hours results in an exact \(20\%\) increase in total cost. Combining both results yields **Rs. 504; 20%**, which matches choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. \pounds 504; 20\%}}\]
Key points
  • Energy values are computed using the relation \(\text{kWh} = \dfrac{\text{Watts} \times \text{Hours}}{1000}\). Because cost depends linearly on duration, any percentage shift in operational hours translates directly into an identical percentage shift in cost.

questions.question:
A bag contains Violet (V), Yellow (Y), Red (R), and Green (G) balls. On counting them, the following results are obtained:
  1. The sum of Yellow balls and twice the number of Violet balls is 50.
  2. The sum of Violet and Green balls is 50.
  3. The sum of Yellow and Red balls is 50.
  4. The sum of Violet and twice the number of Red balls is 50.
Which one of the following Pie charts correctly represents the balls in the bag?
questions.explanation:
Let \(V, Y, R,\) and \(G\) represent the number of Violet, Yellow, Red, and Green balls in the bag, respectively. We write out the four provided linear conditions as equations: \[\begin{aligned} \text{(1)} \quad Y + 2V &= 50 \\ \text{(2)} \quad V + G &= 50 \implies G = 50 - V \\ \text{(3)} \quad Y + R &= 50 \implies R = 50 - Y \\ \text{(4)} \quad V + 2R &= 50 \end{aligned}\] Let us isolate the variables by substituting equation (3) into equation (4): \[V + 2(50 - Y) = 50 \implies V + 100 - 2Y = 50 \implies 2Y - V = 50\] Now, create a \(2 \times 2\) system using this new relation alongside equation (1): \[\begin{aligned} Y + 2V &= 50 \implies 2Y + 4V = 100 \\ 2Y - V &= 50 \end{aligned}\] Subtract the second equation from the first multiplied equation: \[(2Y + 4V) - (2Y - V) = 100 - 50 \implies 5V = 50 \implies V = 10\] Substitute \(V = 10\) back into our equations to solve for the remaining ball counts: \[Y + 2(10) = 50 \implies Y + 20 = 50 \implies Y = 30\] \[G = 50 - V = 50 - 10 \implies G = 40\] \[R = 50 - Y = 50 - 30 \implies R = 20\] The total number of balls in the bag is: \[\text{Total} = V + Y + R + G = 10 + 30 + 20 + 40 = 100 \text{ balls}\] Because the total ball count is exactly 100, the count of each color maps directly to its percentage value in a pie chart: \[V = 10\%, \quad Y = 30\%, \quad R = 20\%, \quad G = 40\%\] Looking at the options, **Pie Chart A** displays these exact percentage allocations for all four sectors. \[\boxed{\text{A}}\]
Key points
  • System equations are solved by using substitution to eliminate variables one by one. When the total item count equals 100, the individual quantities convert directly into percentages for pie chart mapping.

questions.question: Consider a five-digit number PQRST that has distinct digits P, Q, R, S, and T, and satisfies the following conditions: \[P < Q\] \[S > P > T\] \[R < T\] If integers 1 through 5 are used to construct such a number, the value of P is:
questions.explanation:
We need to find the value of digit \(P\) in a five-digit number \(PQRST\) made of distinct digits chosen from the set of integers \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}\). Let us list the three conditional inequalities provided: \[\begin{aligned} \text{(1)} \quad P &< Q \\ \text{(2)} \quad S &> P > T \\ \text{(3)} \quad R &< T \end{aligned}\] Let us combine these separate conditions into a single continuous chain of inequalities: From condition (2), we have \(S > P > T\). From condition (3), we have \(T > R\), which gives: \[S > P > T > R\] This chain ranks four of our five distinct digits in a strict order: \(S\) is the largest, followed by \(P\), then \(T\), and \(R\) is the smallest. Now let us find where the remaining digit \(Q\) fits into this hierarchy using condition (1):
  • Condition (1) states \(Q > P\). This means \(Q\) must be larger than \(P\), so it can only occupy positions above \(P\) alongside \(S\).
  • Since \(P\) must be strictly greater than both \(T\) and \(R\) (\(P > T > R\)), there must be at least **two distinct digits** strictly smaller than \(P\).
  • In our available set of five integers \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}\), the only digit that has exactly two integers smaller than it (\(1\) and \(2\)) is **3**.
Therefore, \(P\) must equal 3. The digits smaller than \(P\) are assigned to \(T\) and \(R\) (\(T=2, R=1\)), while the digits larger than \(P\) are assigned to \(S\) and \(Q\) (\(4\) and \(5\)). This satisfies all conditions and matches choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 3}}\]
Key points
  • Solve inequality puzzles by linking separate conditions into a single continuous chain. This reveals the relative rank of each variable and isolates its possible integer values.

questions.question: A business person buys potatoes of two different varieties P and Q, mixes them in a certain ratio and sells them at ₹ 192 per kg. The cost of the variety P is ₹ 800 for 5 kg. The cost of the variety Q is ₹ 800 for 4 kg. If the person gets 8% profit, what is the P:Q ratio (by weight)?
questions.explanation:
A business person buys potatoes of varieties P and Q, mixes them, and sells the mixture for Rs. 192 per kg while earning an \(8\%\) profit. Step 1: Calculate the cost price of the mixture (\(C_m\))
The selling price is \(SP = \text{Rs. } 192/\text{kg}\) at a profit of \(8\%\): \[SP = C_m \times (1 + \text{Profit Rate}) \implies 192 = C_m \times 1.08\] \[C_m = \dfrac{192}{1.08} = \dfrac{19200}{108} = \dfrac{1600}{9} \approx \text{Rs. } 177.78/\text{kg}\] Step 2: Calculate the individual cost prices per kg (\(C_P\) and \(C_Q\))
  • **Variety P:** Costs Rs. 800 for 5 kg \(\implies C_P = \dfrac{800}{5} = \text{Rs. } 160/\text{kg}\).
  • **Variety Q:** Costs Rs. 800 for 4 kg \(\implies C_Q = \dfrac{800}{4} = \text{Rs. } 200/\text{kg}\).
Step 3: Apply the Alligation Cross Method to find the weight ratio \(W_P : W_Q\)
\[\dfrac{W_P}{W_Q} = \dfrac{C_Q - C_m}{C_m - C_P}\] Substitute our calculated cost values into the ratio equation: \[\dfrac{W_P}{W_Q} = \dfrac{200 - \frac{1600}{9}}{\frac{1600}{9} - 160} = \dfrac{\frac{1800 - 1600}{9}}{\frac{1600 - 1440}{9}} = \dfrac{200}{160}\] Simplify this fraction by dividing both terms by their greatest common divisor (40): \[\dfrac{W_P}{W_Q} = \dfrac{5}{4} \implies W_P : W_Q = 5:4\] This matches choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 5:4}}\]
Key points
  • Mixture problems are solved by finding the cost price from the selling price and profit margin, then applying the alligation ratio formula: \(\frac{W_1}{W_2} = \frac{C_2 - C_m}{C_m - C_1}\).

questions.question: Three villages P, Q, and R are located in such a way that the distance PQ = 13 km, QR = 14 km, and RP = 15 km, as shown in the figure. A straight road joins Q and R. It is proposed to connect P to this road QR by constructing another road. What is the minimum possible length (in km) of this connecting road?
questions.explanation:
Three villages P, Q, and R form a triangle with side lengths \(PQ = 13\text{ km}\), \(QR = 14\text{ km}\), and \(RP = 15\text{ km}\). We need to find the minimum possible length of a road connecting village P to the straight road QR. The shortest distance from a point to a straight line is the perpendicular segment dropped from that point onto the line. Therefore, the minimum length of the connecting road corresponds exactly to the **altitude (height \(h\)) of \(\triangle PQR\)** dropped from vertex P onto the base side QR. Let us calculate the total area of \(\triangle PQR\) using **Heron's Formula**: First, compute the semi-perimeter \(s\): \[s = \dfrac{PQ + QR + RP}{2} = \dfrac{13 + 14 + 15}{2} = \dfrac{42}{2} = 21\text{ km}\] Now, substitute \(s = 21\) into Heron's area equation: \[\text{Area} = \sqrt{s(s - PQ)(s - QR)(s - RP)}\] \[\text{Area} = \sqrt{21 \times (21 - 13) \times (21 - 14) \times (21 - 15)}\] \[\text{Area} = \sqrt{21 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6}\] \[\text{Area} = \sqrt{(7 \times 3) \times 8 \times 7 \times (2 \times 3)}\] \[\text{Area} = \sqrt{7^2 \times 3^2 \times 16} = 7 \times 3 \times 4 = 84\text{ km}^2\] We can also express the area of a triangle using its base and height: \[\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{Base} \times \text{Height} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times QR \times h\] Set this equal to our calculated area value (\(84\text{ km}^2\)) and solve for the height \(h\): \[84 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 14 \times h \implies 84 = 7h \implies h = \dfrac{84}{7} = 12\text{ km}\] The minimum length of the connecting road is exactly \(12.0\text{ km}\). This matches choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 12.0}}\]
Key points
  • The shortest distance from a vertex to the opposite side of a triangle is its perpendicular altitude. This height is found easily by computing the triangle's area via Heron's formula and substituting it into the standard area equation: \(\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}\).
